questions.stem: A 37 year old woman with pernicious anaemia has 2 months of tiredness, poor appetite and a dull ache under her right ribs. She drinks 4 units of alcohol a week and takes no other medicines. Her temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Hepatitis B and C serology are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A woman with another autoimmune disease, an ALT-dominant rise and raised IgG has autoimmune hepatitis. PBC would give a cholestatic picture with a raised ALP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Female, another autoimmune disease, hepatitic LFTs with high IgG and viral causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: 4 units a week is far too little to cause liver disease.
Gives a mild ALT rise with obesity and metabolic risk, not an IgG of 24.

Cholestatic, associated with ulcerative colitis; ALP dominant.

steps.x: **B. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Autoimmune disease + ALT-dominant LFTs + high IgG in a woman = autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has deranged liver tests found at a well-woman check. She has vitiligo and her mother has autoimmune thyroid disease. She feels well. Viral hepatitis serology is negative. Antinuclear antibody and anti-smooth muscle antibody are positive; anti-LKM antibody is negative.

questions.e: ANA and ASMA positivity in an adult with personal and family autoimmunity is type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. Type 2 is anti-LKM positive.

Adult woman, autoimmune background, ANA plus ASMA positive, anti-LKM negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: No new medicine is mentioned and it would not give ASMA.
Antimitochondrial antibody and raised ALP, not ASMA.
Defined by anti-LKM, which is negative here.
Presents under 40 with neuropsychiatric signs and low caeruloplasmin.

steps.x: **C. Type 1 autoimmune hepatitis.** ANA + ASMA = type 1; anti-LKM = type 2.

questions.stem: A 14 year old girl has 3 weeks of jaundice and tiredness. She has had type 1 diabetes since age 6. Her temperature is 37.3°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 106/64 mmHg. Viral serology is negative. ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody are negative. Anti-liver/kidney microsomal type 1 antibody is strongly positive.

questions.e: A girl with anti-LKM positivity and negative ANA/ASMA has type 2 autoimmune hepatitis, which tends to be more aggressive.

steps.x: Young female, autoimmune diabetes, anti-LKM positive with ANA/ASMA negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: Excluded by negative viral serology.
Unconjugated bilirubin only, with normal ALT.
Cholestatic, linked to ulcerative colitis, with p-ANCA.
Would be ANA and ASMA positive.

steps.x: **E. Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.** Anti-LKM in a child or young woman = type 2 autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman has 10 days of jaundice, nausea, aching knees and right upper quadrant pain. She has not travelled and takes the combined pill only. She has a tender, enlarged liver. Hepatitis A IgM, hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis E IgM are negative. Her IgG is 26 g/L (6–16) and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Autoimmune hepatitis can present like an acute hepatitis in a young woman; negative viral serology with high IgG and ASMA confirms the autoimmune cause.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Acute hepatitis picture with arthralgia, but viral tests negative, IgG high and ASMA positive.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: Gives fever and Murphy's sign with a cholestatic, not hepatitic, picture.
Excluded by a negative hepatitis A IgM.
Mild unconjugated jaundice with a normal ALT.
Sore throat and lymphadenopathy; would not give ASMA and high IgG.

steps.x: **C. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Acute hepatitis + negative viral serology + high IgG + ASMA = autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue and malaise. Her brother has Graves' disease and her father has type 1 diabetes. She has coeliac disease. She drinks rarely. Her BMI is 22. Her ALT is 290 IU/L (10–50), ALP 128 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 21 g/L (6–16). Hepatitis B and C tests are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her abnormal liver tests?
questions.e: Personal and first-degree family autoimmunity with ALT-dominant LFTs and high IgG points to autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Strong personal and family autoimmune history, hepatitic LFTs and raised IgG.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: Malabsorption gives anaemia and weight loss, not an ALT of 290 with high IgG.
Gives raised ferritin and transferrin saturation, usually in men; IgG is not raised.
Unlikely with a BMI of 22 and does not raise IgG.
ALP would dominate, with itch and raised IgM.

steps.x: **A. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Family Graves'/T1DM + own coeliac + hepatitic LFTs + high IgG = autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 48 year old woman with type 1 autoimmune hepatitis stopped her treatment 5 years ago. She now has abdominal swelling, ankle oedema and easy bruising. She has spider naevi, palmar erythema and shifting dullness. Her albumin is 26 g/L (35–50), INR 1.8 and platelets 82 × 10⁹/L (150–400).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her current findings?
questions.e: Untreated autoimmune hepatitis drives fibrosis and cirrhosis: stigmata of chronic liver disease, low albumin, raised INR and low platelets from portal hypertension.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Long untreated autoimmune liver disease with stigmata of chronic liver disease and portal hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Cirrhosis.

elim: Develops over days to weeks in a previously healthy liver, with encephalopathy.
Hepatic vein thrombosis gives sudden pain and tender hepatomegaly; no reason here.
Would not cause spider naevi, raised INR or low platelets.
Raised JVP; would not cause spider naevi or thrombocytopenia.

steps.x: **C. Cirrhosis.** Untreated autoimmune hepatitis → fibrosis → cirrhosis; transplant is the option once advanced.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with autoimmune thyroid disease has 6 weeks of fatigue. She is not jaundiced. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 70 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. Abdominal examination is normal. Her liver tests are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely pattern of liver injury?
o: Cholestatic, with ALP much higher than ALT
Hepatocellular, with ALT much higher than ALP
questions.e: Autoimmune hepatitis attacks hepatocytes, giving deranged transaminases with a normal or only slightly raised ALP.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Woman with autoimmune disease; ALT 340 against ALP 120.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Hepatocellular, with ALT much higher than ALP.

elim: That is PBC or PSC; here ALP is only just above normal.
Points to alcohol or enzyme induction, not a hepatocyte attack.
Bilirubin is normal and the ALT is high.
ALT is raised and albumin is normal.

steps.x: **B. Hepatocellular, with ALT much higher than ALP.** Autoimmune hepatitis = hepatitic (ALT-dominant) pattern, ALP normal or mildly raised.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman has autoimmune hepatitis diagnosed after routine bloods showed an ALT of 260 IU/L (10–50). She had no symptoms. Her IgG is 20 g/L (6–16) and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive. Her GP reviews her for other conditions that commonly occur with it.
questions.q: Which other condition is she most likely to have or develop?
questions.e: Autoimmune hepatitis clusters with organ-specific autoimmunity: type 1 diabetes, coeliac disease, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo and autoimmune thyroid disease.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.
Asymptomatic type 1 disease found on bloods; associations are organ-specific autoimmune diseases.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Coeliac disease.

elim: HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathy, not a listed association.
Genetic, not autoimmune.
Crystal arthropathy, not autoimmune.
Linked with primary sclerosing cholangitis, not autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: **B. Coeliac disease.** Remember the cluster: T1DM, coeliac, pernicious anaemia, vitiligo, autoimmune thyroid disease.

questions.stem: A 52 year old woman has 6 months of malaise, fatigue and pain in her hands. She has type 1 diabetes. She drinks 2 units a week and has a BMI of 23. Her liver is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin. Hepatitis B, C and E serology, ferritin and caeruloplasmin are normal. Her ALT has been 3 to 6 times the upper limit for 6 months.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A chronic hepatitis with hepatomegaly and arthralgia in a woman with type 1 diabetes, after other causes are excluded, is chronic autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: malaise, fatigue and pain in her hands
palpable 3 cm below the costal margin
steps.x: Chronic hepatitic picture in an autoimmune-prone woman with screening tests for metabolic causes normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Chronic autoimmune hepatitis.

elim: Usually with emphysema; the low alpha-1 antitrypsin level would be the clue.
Normal ferritin excludes it.
Would give symmetrical synovitis, not an ALT 6 times normal.
Normal caeruloplasmin and age over 40 make it unlikely.

steps.x: **B. Chronic autoimmune hepatitis.** Chronic ALT rise + arthralgia + autoimmune history + normal liver screen = chronic autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 23 year old woman has 1 week of jaundice, malaise and dark urine. It began a few days before her period. She has vitiligo. She has had no new sexual partners and no travel. Her temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 112/68 mmHg. Hepatitis A, B and E serology are negative.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: An acute-hepatitis-like illness in a premenstrual young woman with vitiligo and negative viral serology is autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a diagnosis-type answer: build the picture from the history, observations and tests.

clues: a few days before her period
steps.x: Young premenstrual woman, autoimmune disease, acute hepatitis with viral causes excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Autoimmune hepatitis.

Does not cause an ALT of 980 or dark urine.
Gives unconjugated jaundice without a high ALT or dark urine.
Excluded by negative serology.

steps.x: **B. Autoimmune hepatitis.** Acute hepatitis in a premenstrual woman with autoimmunity and negative viral tests = autoimmune hepatitis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with coeliac disease has 2 weeks of jaundice. She returned from India 6 weeks ago. Her ALT is 1300 IU/L (10–50), ALP 150 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 18 g/L (6–16). Anti-smooth muscle antibody is weakly positive. The team suspects autoimmune hepatitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: Viral hepatitis must be excluded before autoimmune hepatitis is confirmed, especially after travel; a weakly positive ASMA can occur in viral hepatitis.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Viral hepatitis serology.

elim: Tests for PBC, which is cholestatic.
Adds little to a hepatitic picture without obstruction.
Comes after viral causes are excluded.
Relevant only under 40 with neurological signs; viral causes are far more likely after travel.

steps.x: **E. Viral hepatitis serology.** Always exclude viral hepatitis before calling it autoimmune.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman has ALT 410 IU/L (10–50), ALP 118 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 23 g/L (6–16). Antinuclear antibody is positive. Viral hepatitis serology is negative. Liver ultrasound shows a normal-sized liver with no biliary dilatation. Her INR is 1.1 and platelets 240 × 10⁹/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Liver biopsy is the gold-standard test for autoimmune hepatitis, used alongside the autoantibody results.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Hepatitic LFTs, high IgG, ANA positive, viruses excluded; the diagnosis now needs confirming.

steps.x: **B. Liver biopsy.** Gold standard for autoimmune hepatitis = liver biopsy, interpreted with autoantibodies.

questions.stem: A 36 year old woman with type 1 diabetes has 1 month of fatigue and jaundice. Her ALT is 620 IU/L (10–50), ALP 132 IU/L (25–115) and IgG 25 g/L (6–16). Viral serology is negative. The hepatologist wants the autoantibody most consistent with the commonest form of autoimmune hepatitis in adults.

questions.e: Anti-smooth muscle antibody (with ANA) is the marker of type 1 autoimmune hepatitis, the commonest adult form.

steps.x: Adult with hepatitic LFTs and high IgG: type 1 disease is the commonest form.

steps.x: Anti-smooth muscle antibody.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman started prednisolone for biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis 3 months ago. She feels better. Her ALT has fallen from 520 to 60 IU/L (10–50). The team wants a second blood test that reflects disease activity and tracks her response to treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate test?
questions.e: IgG is markedly raised in autoimmune hepatitis and falls with treatment, so LFTs and IgG are monitored to track response.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
On treatment; needs a disease-activity marker to pair with LFTs.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has jaundice and an ALT of 480 IU/L (10–50). Her ALP is 140 IU/L (25–115). She has hypothyroidism. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Viral serology and autoantibodies have been sent. An imaging test is needed to look at the liver and exclude biliary obstruction.

Jaundiced woman with a hepatitic picture; first-line imaging needed.

steps.x: Ultrasound of the liver.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the liver.** First imaging in a jaundiced patient = liver ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 16 year old girl has 1 month of lethargy and jaundice. Her ALT is 760 IU/L (10–50) and IgG 24 g/L (6–16). Viral serology is negative. Antinuclear antibody and anti-smooth muscle antibody are both negative. Her paediatric hepatologist still suspects autoimmune hepatitis.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next antibody test?
questions.e: Type 2 autoimmune hepatitis is anti-LKM positive, is more common in girls and young women, and is often ANA/ASMA negative.

steps.x: It asks for a test: decide what question the test must answer at this point.
Young girl, hepatitic picture with high IgG, type 1 antibodies negative.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Anti-liver/kidney microsomal antibody.

Goodpasture's disease marker.
PBC marker.
Autoimmune thyroid disease, not liver.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman has a liver biopsy showing interface hepatitis with plasma cells. Her ALT is 560 IU/L (10–50), IgG 26 g/L (6–16) and anti-smooth muscle antibody is positive. She has no ascites or encephalopathy. Her INR is 1.2. TPMT activity results are awaited.

o: Watch and repeat LFTs in 3 months
questions.e: Immunosuppression with prednisolone is first-line for autoimmune hepatitis and can start while TPMT results are awaited.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has been on prednisolone for autoimmune hepatitis for 2 months. Her ALT has fallen to 70 IU/L (10–50). She has gained 6 kg, has acne and her glucose is rising. Her TPMT activity is normal. She asks how she can reduce her steroid dose.

questions.e: Azathioprine is the steroid-sparing agent, usually in combination, allowing the prednisolone dose to be reduced once TPMT is normal.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.

steps.x: Responding disease, steroid side effects, normal TPMT: time for a steroid-sparing drug.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Add azathioprine.

elim: Not the standard second-line agent.
No role in autoimmune hepatitis.
She is responding well.
Abrupt withdrawal risks relapse and adrenal crisis.

steps.x: **A. Add azathioprine.** Steroid-sparing therapy in autoimmune hepatitis = azathioprine (check TPMT first).

questions.stem: A 26 year old woman with autoimmune hepatitis has responded to prednisolone. Her hepatologist plans to add azathioprine to reduce her steroid dose. Her full blood count is normal: haemoglobin 128 g/L (115–165), white cell count 6.2 × 10⁹/L (4–11) and platelets 260 × 10⁹/L (150–400).

questions.e: Azathioprine is metabolised by TPMT; low activity causes severe myelosuppression at standard doses, so TPMT activity is measured first.

About to start a thiopurine with a normal baseline count.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman has had type 1 autoimmune hepatitis for 3 years on azathioprine and low-dose prednisolone. She feels well. Her ALT is 32 IU/L (10–50) and IgG 13 g/L (6–16). She asks whether she can stop her tablets because she is better.

o: Continue maintenance immunosuppression and monitor LFTs and IgG
Switch azathioprine to prednisolone alone at a high dose
questions.e: Autoimmune hepatitis needs maintenance immunosuppression with monitoring of LFTs and IgG; stopping often leads to relapse.

In remission on maintenance therapy; normal ALT and IgG.

steps.x: Continue maintenance immunosuppression and monitor LFTs and IgG.

steps.x: **B. Continue maintenance immunosuppression and monitor LFTs and IgG.** Long-term: maintenance immunosuppression + monitor LFTs and IgG.

questions.stem: A 50 year old woman has type 1 autoimmune hepatitis. Despite 8 years of prednisolone and azathioprine, she now has cirrhosis with diuretic-resistant ascites and two admissions with variceal bleeding. Her bilirubin is 90 μmol/L (<17), albumin 24 g/L (35–50) and INR 2.0.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.e: Advanced, decompensated or refractory autoimmune hepatitis needs liver transplant assessment.

steps.x: It asks for management: decide the stage of the illness and what comes next.
Refractory disease that has progressed to decompensated cirrhosis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Referral for liver transplant assessment.

More steroid will not reverse decompensated cirrhosis.
Can worsen autoimmune hepatitis.

steps.x: **C. Referral for liver transplant assessment.** Advanced or refractory autoimmune hepatitis = liver transplant.

questions.stem: A 29 year old woman has biopsy-proven autoimmune hepatitis. The biopsy shows dense lymphocytes and plasma cells at the junction of the portal tracts and the liver lobule, with hepatocytes being destroyed. Viral tests are negative. She asks why her immune system is attacking her liver.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Bile acid toxicity from obstructed ducts
Immune complex deposition from a chronic viral infection
Loss of self-tolerance with autoreactive T-cells targeting hepatocyte antigens
questions.e: Autoimmune hepatitis results from a breakdown of self-tolerance: autoreactive T-cells and autoantibodies target hepatocyte antigens, driving ongoing inflammation.

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying process.
Lymphocytic attack on hepatocytes with no virus present.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Loss of self-tolerance with autoreactive T-cells targeting hepatocyte antigens.

elim: Cholestatic disease; the attack here is on hepatocytes.
Wilson's disease.

Haemochromatosis.

steps.x: **E. Loss of self-tolerance with autoreactive T-cells targeting hepatocyte antigens.** Autoimmune hepatitis = loss of self-tolerance → autoreactive T-cells attack hepatocytes.

questions.stem: A 44 year old woman has had poorly controlled autoimmune hepatitis for 10 years. A repeat liver biopsy now shows bands of collagen bridging portal tracts and regenerative nodules. Her ALT remains about 3 times the upper limit of normal.
questions.q: Which cell is mainly responsible for the collagen deposition?
questions.e: Chronic immune-mediated inflammation activates hepatic stellate cells, which lay down collagen, causing fibrosis and cirrhosis.

steps.x: Long-standing inflammation now producing fibrosis and nodules: cirrhosis.

steps.x: Hepatic stellate cell.

steps.x: **B. Hepatic stellate cell.** Fibrosis in chronic liver inflammation = activated hepatic stellate cells.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has autoimmune hepatitis. Her total protein is 92 g/L (60–80) with a normal albumin. Serum protein electrophoresis shows a broad increase in the gamma region with no discrete band. Her IgG is 31 g/L (6–16).
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for her raised IgG?

steps.x: It asks for the mechanism: link the finding in the stem to the underlying process.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with autoimmune hepatitis started azathioprine 4 weeks ago at a standard dose. Her TPMT was not checked. She now has mouth ulcers, a sore throat and bruising. o: Accumulation of thioguanine nucleotides from low TPMT activity
questions.e: With low TPMT activity, azathioprine is shunted to cytotoxic thioguanine nucleotides, causing severe myelosuppression and pancytopenia at standard doses.

steps.x: Accumulation of thioguanine nucleotides from low TPMT activity.

steps.x: **A. Accumulation of thioguanine nucleotides from low TPMT activity.** Low TPMT + azathioprine = toxic metabolites → pancytopenia; test TPMT first.

questions.stem: A 13 year old girl and a 46 year old woman are both diagnosed with autoimmune hepatitis in the same clinic. The girl is anti-LKM positive and presented with acute liver failure. The woman is ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive and has autoimmune thyroid disease.

Type 2 disease is caused by a virus
Type 2 disease is more common in children and tends to be more aggressive

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Type 2 disease is more common in children and tends to be more aggressive.
